regression.text:
The writer uses the tuning of the piano to present a family that treats Femi's absence as a small, repairable fault.

The mother's words, "Just the A" and "It's only the A that's gone", reduce the loss to a single note, and the word "only" returns in the narrator's correction, "It was not only the A." Conventionally, "only" limits a claim to one item, so the mother's wording makes the loss seem contained. Against that account, the piano has gone "one key at a time", the way a house goes cold, from "the rooms nobody uses" to "the kitchen where everyone sits". The lid, left up because "closing it would have meant deciding something", suggests that the household avoids a decision that would acknowledge the loss.

The phrase "two strings that would not agree" and the tuner's diagnosis, "They just stop listening to each other", give the instrument a will of its own, a personification that moves the family's breakdown into the piano. Conventionally, listening means attending to another's voice, so the family, like its piano, has stopped attending to one another. The clean note travels "up the stairs to the room with the posters still on the wall", most likely Femi's room, and "nobody said anything until it had stopped". The silence suggests a family that listens to the note but not to each other.

The mother's last words, "He'll want it in tune. When he comes back", turn the repair into a hope of return. The tuning therefore suggests a family that mixes denial with hope, keeping the piano in order so that Femi's absence can seem temporary. Note on(the quotations): every quotation above holds.
